concepts.name: Definition of indefinite integral
concepts.oneLineSummary: ∫ f(x) dx = g(x) + C where g'(x) = f(x); C is arbitrary constant.

concepts.name: Standard integrals of algebraic functions
concepts.oneLineSummary: ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1), ∫ 1/x dx = log|x|, ∫ a^x dx = a^x / log a.

concepts.name: Standard integrals of trigonometric functions
concepts.oneLineSummary: ∫ sin x = −cos x, ∫ cos x = sin x, ∫ sec² x = tan x, ∫ csc² x = −cot x, etc.

concepts.name: Integrals of tan, cot, sec, csc
concepts.oneLineSummary: ∫ tan x = log|sec x|, ∫ cot x = log|sin x|, ∫ sec x = log|sec x + tan x|, ∫ csc x = log|csc x − cot x|.

concepts.name: Integration by substitution (basic)
concepts.oneLineSummary: ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du after u = g(x).

concepts.name: Integrals of the form ∫ dx/(a² ± x²) and √(a² ± x²)
concepts.oneLineSummary: Lead to (1/a) tan^{-1}(x/a), (1/2a) log|(x−a)/(x+a)|, log|x + √(x²±a²)|, sin^{-1}(x/a).

concepts.name: Integration of linear over quadratic
concepts.oneLineSummary: Write numerator as derivative of denominator plus constant; split into log + arctan forms.

concepts.name: t = tan(x/2) substitution (Weierstrass)
concepts.oneLineSummary: Converts rational functions of sin and cos into rational functions of t.

concepts.name: Integration by parts
concepts.oneLineSummary: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du; LIATE rule for choosing u.

concepts.name: Partial fractions
concepts.oneLineSummary: Decompose rational functions into simpler fractions before integrating.

concepts.name: Integrals of the form ∫ (px + q)/(ax² + bx + c) dx
concepts.oneLineSummary: Split into derivative part (log) and constant part (arctan or log).

concepts.name: Integrals involving √(ax² + bx + c)
concepts.oneLineSummary: Complete the square then use standard √(a²±x²) forms.

concepts.name: Trigonometric substitutions
concepts.oneLineSummary: x = a sin θ, a tan θ, a sec θ for √(a²−x²), √(a²+x²), √(x²−a²).

concepts.name: Arbitrary constant C
concepts.oneLineSummary: Always add +C; different antiderivatives differ by a constant.

concepts.name: Common standard forms from notes
concepts.oneLineSummary: The list of basic integrals and the linear-over-quadratic technique.

qna.question: What is the definition of an indefinite integral and why is the constant C necessary?
qna.answer: If g'(x) = f(x) then ∫ f(x) dx = g(x) + C. The constant C appears because the derivative of any constant is zero; different antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant. Omitting C loses a family of solutions.

qna.question: Write the standard integrals of x^n, 1/x and a^x.
qna.answer: ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫ (1/x) dx = log|x| + C; ∫ a^x dx = a^x / log a + C. These are the most frequently used algebraic standard forms.

qna.question: List the basic trigonometric integrals for sin, cos, sec² and csc².
qna.answer: ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C; ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫ sec² x dx = tan x + C; ∫ csc² x dx = −cot x + C. These follow at once by differentiating the right-hand sides.

qna.question: State the integrals of tan x, cot x, sec x and csc x.
qna.answer: ∫ tan x dx = log|sec x| + C; ∫ cot x dx = log|sin x| + C; ∫ sec x dx = log|sec x + tan x| + C; ∫ csc x dx = log|csc x − cot x| + C. Equivalent forms using tan(x/2 + π/4) also exist for sec and csc.

qna.question: Write the four standard integrals involving a² ± x² and their square roots.
qna.answer: ∫ dx/(a² + x²) = (1/a) tan^{-1}(x/a) + C; ∫ dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a) log|(x−a)/(x+a)| + C; ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin^{-1}(x/a) + C; ∫ dx/√(x² ± a²) = log|x + √(x² ± a²)| + C.

qna.question: How do you integrate a linear expression over a quadratic expression?
qna.answer: Write the numerator as a multiple of the derivative of the denominator plus a constant remainder. The integral splits into a logarithm of the quadratic plus a constant times the integral of 1 over the quadratic (which becomes an arctan or log after completing the square).

qna.question: Explain the method of substitution for indefinite integrals.
qna.answer: Choose a new variable u = g(x) so that the integrand becomes f(u) du. Integrate with respect to u and finally substitute back u = g(x). The method works whenever the integrand contains a composite function whose inner derivative is also present (up to a constant factor).

qna.question: State the formula for integration by parts and the usual rule for choosing u.
qna.answer: ∫ u dv = u v − ∫ v du. The LIATE rule (Logarithmic, Inverse trigonometric, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential) suggests the preferred order for selecting the factor u. The goal is to make the remaining integral ∫ v du simpler than the original.

qna.question: When is the substitution t = tan(x/2) useful?
qna.answer: It converts any rational function of sin x and cos x into a rational function of t. Because sin x = 2t/(1+t²), cos x = (1−t²)/(1+t²) and dx = 2 dt/(1+t²), the original trigonometric integral becomes an ordinary rational integral that can be attacked by partial fractions.

qna.question: Integrate √x + 1/√x.
qna.answer: ∫ (x^{1/2} + x^{-1/2}) dx = (2/3) x^{3/2} + 2 x^{1/2} + C. Each term is a standard power integral. The same result is obtained by writing the integrand as (x + 1)/√x and substituting u = √x.

qna.question: Integrate cos 2x.
qna.answer: ∫ cos 2x dx = (1/2) sin 2x + C. The chain rule accounts for the factor 2 inside the cosine; dividing by that factor recovers the correct antiderivative.

qna.question: Evaluate ∫ dx/(9 + x²).
qna.answer: This is the standard form with a = 3: ∫ dx/(a² + x²) = (1/a) tan^{-1}(x/a) + C = (1/3) tan^{-1}(x/3) + C.

qna.question: Evaluate ∫ dx/√(4 − x²).
qna.answer: Standard form ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin^{-1}(x/a) + C with a = 2 gives sin^{-1}(x/2) + C.

qna.question: Integrate tan x.
qna.answer: ∫ tan x dx = ∫ sin x / cos x dx. The substitution u = cos x yields −log|cos x| + C which is the same as log|sec x| + C.

qna.question: Integrate (2x + 3)/(x² + 3x + 2).
qna.answer: The derivative of the denominator is 2x + 3, which matches the numerator exactly. Therefore the integral is simply log|x² + 3x + 2| + C.

qna.question: Integrate x e^x by parts.
qna.answer: Let u = x, dv = e^x dx ⇒ du = dx, v = e^x. Then ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + C = e^x (x − 1) + C.

qna.question: Integrate 2x cos(x²).
qna.answer: Let u = x², du = 2x dx. The integral becomes ∫ cos u du = sin u + C = sin(x²) + C. The factor 2x is precisely the derivative of the inner function.

qna.question: When is the method of partial fractions used?
qna.answer: Partial fractions are used to integrate proper rational functions (degree of numerator less than degree of denominator). The rational function is decomposed into a sum of simpler fractions whose denominators are linear or irreducible quadratic factors; each of those is then integrated by the standard forms.

qna.question: Outline the procedure for integrating an expression containing √(ax² + bx + c).
qna.answer: Complete the square inside the radical so that it becomes √(±(u² ± k²)). Then apply one of the four standard square-root forms (log or inverse sine/tangent). A linear substitution may be needed first to eliminate the linear term.

qna.question: Which trigonometric substitution is appropriate for √(a² − x²)?
qna.answer: x = a sin θ (or x = a cos θ). Then √(a² − x²) = a cos θ and dx = a cos θ dθ, converting the integral into a rational function of sin and cos that can be handled by standard techniques.

qna.question: Why must the arbitrary constant always be written?
qna.answer: The indefinite integral represents a whole family of antiderivatives that differ from one another by constants. Writing +C makes this family explicit and is required for full marks in examinations. Omitting C is one of the most common avoidable errors.

qna.question: Evaluate ∫ dx/(x² − 9).
qna.answer: This is ∫ dx/(x² − a²) with a = 3. The formula gives (1/(2·3)) log|(x−3)/(x+3)| + C = (1/6) log|(x−3)/(x+3)| + C.

qna.question: Integrate sec x.
qna.answer: Multiply numerator and denominator by sec x + tan x: ∫ sec x (sec x + tan x)/(sec x + tan x) dx = ∫ (sec² x + sec x tan x)/(sec x + tan x) dx. The numerator is now the derivative of the denominator, so the integral is log|sec x + tan x| + C.

qna.question: Integrate log x by parts.
qna.answer: Let u = log x, dv = dx ⇒ du = dx/x, v = x. Then ∫ log x dx = x log x − ∫ x · (1/x) dx = x log x − ∫ dx = x log x − x + C.

qna.question: Integrate (x + 1)/(x² + 2x + 5).
qna.answer: Derivative of the denominator is 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1). Therefore write the integral as (1/2) ∫ (2x + 2)/(x² + 2x + 5) dx = (1/2) log(x² + 2x + 5) + C. No remainder term appears.

qna.question: Integrate e^{sin x} cos x.
qna.answer: Let u = sin x, du = cos x dx. The integral becomes ∫ e^u du = e^u + C = e^{sin x} + C. The cosine factor is exactly the derivative of the inner function.

qna.question: Integrate sin² x.
qna.answer: Use the identity sin² x = (1 − cos 2x)/2. Then ∫ sin² x dx = ∫ (1/2 − (1/2) cos 2x) dx = x/2 − (1/4) sin 2x + C. Power-reduction identities are the standard route for even powers of sine and cosine.

qna.question: Integrate (3x + 1)/(x² + 1).
qna.answer: Write 3x + 1 = (3/2)(2x) + 1. Then the integral = (3/2) ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx + ∫ 1/(x² + 1) dx = (3/2) log(x² + 1) + tan^{-1} x + C.

qna.question: Evaluate ∫ dx/√(x² + 4).
qna.answer: Standard form ∫ dx/√(x² + a²) = log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C with a = 2 gives log|x + √(x² + 4)| + C.

qna.question: If ∫ f(x) dx = g(x) + C, what is the relation between f and g?
qna.answer: g is an antiderivative of f, i.e., g'(x) = f(x). Conversely, any function whose derivative is f is of the form g(x) + C. This is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in its indefinite-integral form.

qna.question: Convert ∫ dx/(sin x + cos x) into a rational integral using t = tan(x/2).
qna.answer: sin x = 2t/(1+t²), cos x = (1−t²)/(1+t²), dx = 2 dt/(1+t²). The integrand becomes 2 dt / (2t + 1 − t²) after clearing the common denominator. The resulting rational function of t can be integrated by completing the square or partial fractions.

qna.question: Integrate 1/√(x² + 2x + 2).
qna.answer: Complete the square: x² + 2x + 2 = (x+1)² + 1. Let u = x + 1. The integral becomes ∫ du/√(u² + 1) = log|u + √(u² + 1)| + C = log|x + 1 + √(x² + 2x + 2)| + C.

qna.question: A student integrates 1/(x² + 1) as log(x² + 1). What is the error?
qna.answer: The correct antiderivative is tan^{-1} x, not the logarithm. The logarithm appears only when the quadratic under the integral has the form x² − a² or when the numerator is the derivative of the denominator. Confusing the two standard forms is a frequent mistake.

qna.question: Integrate x² e^x by parts twice.
qna.answer: First: u = x², dv = e^x dx → x² e^x − ∫ 2x e^x dx. Second: u = 2x, dv = e^x dx → x² e^x − 2x e^x + ∫ 2 e^x dx = e^x (x² − 2x + 2) + C. Repeated integration by parts systematically reduces the power of x.

qna.question: Integrate 1/(x log x).
qna.answer: Let u = log x, du = dx/x. The integral becomes ∫ du/u = log|u| + C = log|log x| + C. The substitution works because the derivative of the inner logarithm appears in the numerator.

qna.question: Integrate csc x.
qna.answer: Multiply numerator and denominator by csc x − cot x: ∫ csc x (csc x − cot x)/(csc x − cot x) dx = ∫ (csc² x − csc x cot x)/(csc x − cot x) dx. The numerator is the derivative of the denominator (up to sign), yielding log|csc x − cot x| + C.

qna.question: Two students obtain different-looking answers for the same indefinite integral. How can both be correct?
qna.answer: Their answers differ by a constant. Because the derivative of a constant is zero, both expressions are valid antiderivatives. Checking by differentiation or by examining the difference of the two answers confirms they are equivalent up to a constant.
